claims.text: Retention of toughness in high-entropy alloys is governed by the thermal stability of a single-phase FCC matrix.
Controlled annealing determines whether brittle intermetallic precipitates form.
Under optimum thermal conditions, the FCC matrix remains stable.
A stable FCC matrix effectively absorbs deformation energy.
A slight increase in annealing temperature causes brittle phases to nucleate.
Brittle phases act as crack-initiation sites and reduce toughness.
The proposed initial material has a mostly single-phase FCC microstructure with minimal secondary-phase content.
Increasing annealing temperature or time slightly above the optimum condition is the controlled intervention.
The structural mediator is the formation of brittle intermetallic precipitates at grain boundaries or within grains.
Solid-solution strengthening under optimum annealing maintains a metastable, ductile FCC matrix that resists crack propagation.
A modest increase in annealing temperature accelerates phase-separation kinetics.
Accelerated phase separation produces brittle-phase precipitation.
Brittle precipitates disrupt continuity of the ductile matrix and create stress concentrations.
Matrix disruption and precipitate-induced stress concentrations reduce alloy toughness.
Relative to the baseline, a slightly higher annealing temperature will produce microscopy-detectable brittle precipitates.
Relative to the baseline, a slightly higher annealing temperature will cause a statistically significant reduction in measured toughness.
The proposed mechanism is expected to apply primarily to similar compositional spaces and processing histories in which an FCC phase predominates.
In inherently multiphase compositions or under high-strain-rate or very-low-temperature deformation, the governing mechanism may differ.
Thermal thresholds and precipitation kinetics vary with alloy composition and grain size.
